title: Best sellers for the price watch

brief.decision: Which products go on the weekly competitor price watch list for the second half of 2025
brief.deadline: The pricing team's planning meeting at the start of July 2025

expected_output.grain: one row per product kept: the 3 best sellers of each category by net revenue from January to June 2025

checkpoints.prompt: Joost, the pricing lead, wants the 3 best-selling products of each category by net revenue from January to June 2025: exactly 3 per category, the lower product_id first when products tie on net revenue, each with its share of the net revenue of its whole category in that period. Before you write any SQL, which plan returns that?

options.text: Total each product's net revenue, number each category's products from the highest down with the lower product_id first on ties, keep places 1 to 3, then divide each kept product by the total of the 3 kept.

Number every order line of each category from the highest line revenue down with the lower product_id first on ties, keep places 1 to 3, then add up each product's kept lines and divide by its category's total.

Total each product's net revenue, then number each category's products from the highest down with the lower product_id first on ties and take the category's total over all its products; then keep places 1 to 3.

Total each product's net revenue, rank each category's products from the highest down so that tied products share a place, keep every product ranked 1 to 3, and divide each by its category's total over all its products.

checkpoints.prompt: Joost first wants to know how many products the list is chosen from. How many different products have at least one order line in the orders with an order_ts from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 up to but not including 2025-07-01 00:00:00 (order_ts holds UTC time)? Count each product once, however many lines it has. Type a whole number.
Write the query that answers Joost's question.

Joost's headline: take the orders with an order_ts from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 up to but not including 2025-07-01 00:00:00 (order_ts holds UTC time). A product's net revenue is the sum of quantity times unit_price_eur minus line_discount_eur over its lines in those orders. In each category, the top 3 are the 3 products with the highest net revenue; when products tie on net revenue, the lower product_id comes first, and a category with fewer than 3 products that sold keeps them all. What percentage of the net revenue of all those orders came from the top 3 products of every category together? Type the percentage rounded to 1 decimal, for example 12.3.
Joost's result for January to June 2025 shows that in most categories the 3 best sellers brought in more than half of the category's net revenue. What can Joost conclude from this result alone?

options.text: These products sold best because they were cheaper than at the competitors, so keeping their prices where they are will keep their sales.
Revenue sits in a few products per category, so watching their prices covers much of it; the result cannot show how their sales react to competitors' prices.
The products outside the top 3 bring in little revenue, so their prices can go up in the second half without losing any sales.
The same products will lead their categories for the rest of 2025, so the watch list will not need an update before next year.

checkpoints.prompt: Write 2 to 4 sentences for Joost: the headline number, what it means for the weekly price watch list, one caveat and one next step.

model_plan:
Metric formula: net_revenue_eur, the sum of quantity times unit_price_eur minus line_discount_eur over a product's lines; revenue_rank, its place in its category from the highest net revenue down; category_share_pct, 100 times its net revenue divided by the net revenue of all the products of its category.
Output grain: one row per product kept, at most 3 per category.
Tables and keys: order_lines joined to orders on order_id and to products on product_id, in a step at one row per product; a window step places and totals each category's products; categories joined on category_id for the name.
Filters: order_ts from 2025-01-01 up to but not including 2025-07-01, in UTC; places 1 to 3, kept in an outer query after the window step.
Edge cases: products that tie on net revenue take their places by product_id, so each category keeps exactly 3; a category with fewer than 3 products that sold keeps them all; the share divides by the whole category, not by the 3 kept.
Expected row count: 120
model_answer_template: From January to June 2025, the 3 best sellers of each category brought in {CP4} percent of all net revenue, out of {CP2} products that sold. A short weekly watch list therefore covers much of the revenue that a competitor's price move could hit. The list shows where revenue sat in one half year, not how sensitive these products are to price, and the second half brings Black Friday and the holidays, when the leaders can change. Next, check each listed product's price against its latest competitor price checks every week, and refresh the list each quarter.
follow_up_question: How does each listed product's price compare with its latest competitor price checks?
